name: Smart Parking Assistant
description: Build a parking distance helper using an ultrasonic sensor, RGB LED colours, and a buzzer that beeps faster as you get closer.
guide:
What you will build

A small sensor unit that shows green when a space is clear, yellow when a vehicle is approaching, and red with fast beeps when you are too close — like parking sensors on cars.

What you will learn

  • How ultrasonic sensors measure distance in centimetres
  • How RGB LEDs combine red, green, and blue channels
  • How feedback frequency helps drivers park safely

Safety first

  • Power off before rewiring
  • Keep buzzer volume reasonable during classroom tests

You did it when…

  • LED shows green beyond 50 cm, yellow between 30–50 cm, red below 30 cm
  • Buzzer beeps faster as distance decreases
  • Readings are stable when you hold a book at a fixed distance

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Wire HC-SR04
    Connect VCC to 5 V, GND to GND, Trig to pin 10, Echo to pin 11.
  2. Wire common-cathode RGB LED
    Red pin through 220 Ω to pin 6, green to 5, blue to 4. Common cathode to GND.
  3. Connect buzzer
    Buzzer positive to pin 8, negative to GND.
  4. Test distance function
    Upload a sketch that prints distance to Serial Monitor. Verify values change when you move your hand.
  5. Add colour zones
    If distance > 50 cm: green ON. If 30–50 cm: yellow (red+green). If < 30 cm: red ON and buzzer with delay mapped to distance.
  6. Mount in a box
    Face sensor outward like a parking aid. Label green/yellow/red zones on a card for demonstration.
  7. Demonstrate
    Move a cardboard “car” toward the sensor. Explain how this reduces collisions in tight spaces.

Code to upload

Parking distance feedback (Arduino C)

const int TRIG=10, ECHO=11;
const int R=6, G=5, B=4, BUZZ=8;

long distCm() {
  digitalWrite(TRIG,LOW); delayMicroseconds(2);
  digitalWrite(TRIG,HIGH); delayMicroseconds(10);
  digitalWrite(TRIG,LOW);
  return pulseIn(ECHO,HIGH,30000)/58;
}

void setRGB(int r,int g,int b){
  digitalWrite(R,r); digitalWrite(G,g); digitalWrite(B,b);
}

void setup(){
  pinMode(TRIG,OUTPUT); pinMode(ECHO,INPUT);
  pinMode(R,OUTPUT); pinMode(G,OUTPUT); pinMode(B,OUTPUT);
  pinMode(BUZZ,OUTPUT);
  Serial.begin(9600);
}

void loop(){
  long d=distCm();
  Serial.println(d);
  if(d>50){ setRGB(0,1,0); noTone(BUZZ); }
  else if(d>30){ setRGB(1,1,0); tone(BUZZ,400); delay(300); noTone(BUZZ); }
  else { setRGB(1,0,0); tone(BUZZ,800); delay(100); noTone(BUZZ); }
  delay(100);
}

codes.title: Parking distance feedback
codes.description: Expand with RGB zones after distance works.

name: Solar Tracker System
description: Build a two-axis solar panel tracker that follows the brightest light using four LDR sensors and two servo motors.
guide:
What you will build

A small solar panel (or panel model) mounted on servos that rotates toward the strongest light source — mimicking sun-tracking systems used in solar farms.

What you will learn

  • How LDR sensors compare light intensity in different directions
  • How servos provide controlled rotation
  • Why tracking the sun increases solar energy capture

Safety first

  • Do not look directly at bright lamps used for testing
  • Secure servos firmly — sudden movement can pinch fingers

You did it when…

  • Panel turns toward a desk lamp when you move it left or right
  • Both horizontal and vertical axes respond without jitter
  • You explain when tracking helps most (clear sky vs cloudy)

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Mount four LDRs
    Place LDRs on left, right, top, and bottom of a small panel frame. Each forms a voltage divider into analog pins A0–A3.
  2. Attach two servos
    One servo for azimuth (left-right), one for elevation (up-down). Use a cardboard bracket.
  3. Read and compare LDR values
    Upload test code printing all four readings. Cover one LDR — its value should drop noticeably.
  4. Implement tracking logic
    If left > right + threshold, increment azimuth servo angle. If right > left, decrement. Repeat for top/bottom on elevation servo.
  5. Add dead band
    Only move when difference exceeds 30–50 analog units to stop constant shaking.
  6. Limit servo range
    Keep angles between 15° and 165° to avoid cable strain.
  7. Outdoor demo (optional)
    On a sunny day, observe slow tracking. Log angle changes every 10 minutes.

Code to upload

Dual-axis light tracker (simplified) (Arduino C)

#include <Servo.h>
Servo azimuth, elevation;
const int L= A0, R= A1, T= A2, B= A3;
int az=90, el=90;
const int TH=40;

void setup(){
  azimuth.attach(9); elevation.attach(10);
  azimuth.write(az); elevation.write(el);
  Serial.begin(9600);
}

void loop(){
  int l=analogRead(L), r=analogRead(R), t=analogRead(T), b=analogRead(B);
  if(l>r+TH && az<165) az++;
  if(r>l+TH && az>15) az--;
  if(t>b+TH && el<165) el++;
  if(b>t+TH && el>15) el--;
  azimuth.write(az); elevation.write(el);
  delay(50);
}

name: RFID Access Control System
description: Create a door-lock demo that opens a servo latch when an authorised RFID card is scanned and denies unknown cards.
guide:
What you will build

An RFID reader that unlocks a model door (servo latch) for registered cards and flashes a red LED for unknown cards.

What you will learn

  • How RFID tags send unique IDs wirelessly
  • How access control lists work in security systems
  • How actuators (servos) respond to digital decisions

Safety first

  • Do not use on real school doors without teacher approval
  • Keep servo fingers clear during testing

You did it when…

  • Authorised card opens latch within 2 seconds
  • Unknown card triggers red LED and buzzer, latch stays closed
  • You can add a second authorised card in code

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Install MFRC522 library
    In Arduino IDE Library Manager, search MFRC522 and install.
  2. Wire RC522 module
    SDA→10, SCK→13, MOSI→11, MISO→12, RST→9, 3.3 V and GND. Use 3.3 V if module requires it.
  3. Wire servo and LEDs
    Green LED pin 7, red LED pin 6, servo signal pin 5. Servo locked at 0°, open at 90°.
  4. Scan and record authorised UID
    Run example DumpInfo sketch. Tap your card and copy the UID hex string into your code array.
  5. Program access check
    On successful read, compare UID to allowed list. Match → servo open 3 s. No match → red blink + buzzer.
  6. Build door model
    Cardboard door with servo as bolt. Test 10 scans — no false accepts.

Code to upload

RFID door latch (concept) (Arduino C)

Requires MFRC522 library. Replace UID bytes with your card values from DumpInfo.

// After reading card UID into uid[]:
// if uid matches authorised card:
//   servo.write(90); delay(3000); servo.write(0);
// else:
//   digitalWrite(RED_LED, HIGH); tone(BUZZ, 600, 500);

name: Smart Street Lighting System
description: Automate a model street lamp that turns on only when it is dark and motion is detected nearby.
guide:
What you will build

A lamp that stays off in daylight, stays off at night until someone walks past (PIR), then lights an LED or bulb for 30 seconds — saving energy like smart city lighting.

What you will learn

  • How to combine two sensors with AND logic
  • How smart cities reduce wasted electricity
  • How timed auto-off prevents lights staying on all night

You did it when…

  • Light never turns on in bright room even if you wave at PIR
  • In dark room, walking past triggers light for ~30 s
  • Light turns off automatically after timeout

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Wire LDR divider to A0
    Measure bright vs dark thresholds in Serial Monitor.
  2. Wire PIR to pin 2
    Wait 60 s warm-up after power-on before testing.
  3. Connect lamp output
    High-power LED or relay-driven bulb on pin 8.
  4. Write combined condition
    if (analogRead(A0) > DARK_THRESHOLD && digitalRead(PIR)==HIGH) turn lamp on and reset 30 s timer.
  5. Test daylight case
    Shine torch on LDR while triggering PIR — lamp must stay off.
  6. Test night case
    Cover LDR, walk past sensor — lamp on then off.
  7. Calculate savings
    Estimate hours saved vs lamp on all night. Write 2 sentences in notebook.

Code to upload

Dark + motion street light (Arduino C)

const int LDR=A0, PIR=2, LAMP=8;
const int DARK=500;
unsigned long onUntil=0;

void setup(){
  pinMode(PIR,INPUT); pinMode(LAMP,OUTPUT);
}

void loop(){
  bool dark = analogRead(LDR) > DARK;
  bool motion = digitalRead(PIR)==HIGH;
  if(dark && motion) onUntil = millis()+30000;
  digitalWrite(LAMP, millis()<onUntil ? HIGH : LOW);
  delay(100);
}

codes.title: Dark + motion street light
codes.description: Tune DARK threshold for your classroom.

name: Fire Detection and Alarm System
description: Detect flame or heat rise with sensors and trigger a loud buzzer and flashing LED alarm.
guide:
What you will build

A tabletop fire alarm demo using a flame sensor and temperature module that sounds when a candle flame (teacher demonstration) or heat source is near.

What you will learn

  • How flame sensors detect infrared light from fire
  • How temperature sensors add a second check
  • Why early detection saves lives and property

Safety first — very important

  • Only teachers handle open flames
  • Keep candle in metal tray with water nearby
  • Test in ventilated area away from smoke detectors
  • Never leave flame unattended

You did it when…

  • Alarm triggers when flame is within sensor range
  • Alarm does not trigger from classroom lights alone
  • Both LED flash and buzzer activate together

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Mount flame sensor
    Digital out to pin 2, VCC and GND. Point sensor toward test area.
  2. Add temperature sensor (optional DHT or LM35 on A0)
    Rising temperature confirms alert.
  3. Wire buzzer and red LED
    Use pin 8 buzzer, pin 9 LED. Flash LED in loop when alarm active.
  4. Calibrate without flame
    Ensure alarm is silent under normal lights. Adjust sensor sensitivity pot if available.
  5. Teacher flame test
    Bring candle toward sensor from 30 cm slowly. Note trigger distance.
  6. Write emergency procedure
    List three steps students should take if they hear a real fire alarm at school.

Code to upload

Flame alarm (Arduino C)

const int FLAME=2, LED=9, BUZZ=8;

void setup(){
  pinMode(FLAME,INPUT);
  pinMode(LED,OUTPUT);
  pinMode(BUZZ,OUTPUT);
}

void loop(){
  if(digitalRead(FLAME)==LOW){ // often LOW = flame detected
    digitalWrite(LED,HIGH);
    tone(BUZZ,1000);
  } else {
    digitalWrite(LED,LOW);
    noTone(BUZZ);
  }
  delay(100);
}

codes.description: Invert LOW/HIGH if your module behaves differently.

name: Automatic Hand Sanitizer Dispenser
description: Build a touchless sanitizer pump that dispenses when your hand is detected within range of an ultrasonic sensor.
guide:
What you will build

A bottle mount with ultrasonic sensor and servo that pushes the pump head once when a hand approaches — no touching the bottle.

What you will learn

  • How touchless systems improve hygiene in hospitals and schools
  • How servos create short mechanical pushes
  • How to debounce triggers so one hand wave = one dispense

Safety first

  • Use water for classroom testing instead of alcohol if open flame nearby
  • Secure bottle so it cannot tip

You did it when…

  • One hand approach gives exactly one pump push
  • System waits 3 s before allowing next dispense
  • No dripping from repeated false triggers

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Mount sanitizer bottle
    Clamp bottle upside-down or sideways with pump facing up. Brace firmly on baseboard.
  2. Position HC-SR04
    Point sensor at where hands will sit, 10–15 cm above nozzle.
  3. Link servo arm to pump
    Cardboard lever pushes pump cap down when servo moves to 70°.
  4. Code distance trigger
    If distance < 12 cm and cooldown expired, move servo down then return.
  5. Add cooldown timer
    After dispense, ignore triggers for 3000 ms.
  6. Test with water
    Count drops per trigger. Adjust servo angle for single dose.

Code to upload

Touchless dispense (Arduino C)

#include <Servo.h>
Servo pump;
const int TRIG=10,ECHO=11;
unsigned long cool=0;

long cm(){
  digitalWrite(TRIG,LOW);delayMicroseconds(2);
  digitalWrite(TRIG,HIGH);delayMicroseconds(10);
  digitalWrite(TRIG,LOW);
  return pulseIn(ECHO,HIGH,30000)/58;
}

void setup(){
  pump.attach(9);
  pinMode(TRIG,OUTPUT); pinMode(ECHO,INPUT);
  pump.write(0);
}

void loop(){
  if(cm()<12 && cm()>0 && millis()-cool>3000){
    pump.write(70); delay(400); pump.write(0); cool=millis();
  }
  delay(100);
}

codes.title: Touchless dispense
codes.description: Add distance read and servo push logic.

name: Robotic Arm with Gripper
description: Build a multi-servo robotic arm with a gripper and control it using a joystick module to pick and place objects.
guide:
What you will build

A 3–4 servo arm (base rotation, shoulder, elbow, gripper) you control with a 2-axis joystick to grab a small block and move it to a target zone.

What you will learn

  • How degrees of freedom let robots reach different positions
  • How joysticks provide analog control input
  • How pick-and-place automation works in factories

Safety first

  • Power off when assembling servo horns
  • Keep clear of moving arm during operation

You did it when…

  • You can pick up a 3 cm cube and release it in a marked zone
  • Each joystick axis maps smoothly to one joint
  • Arm returns to home position without binding

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Assemble arm kit or cardboard arm
    Mount base servo for rotation, shoulder and elbow servos for reach, micro servo for gripper jaws.
  2. Wire servos to pins 5, 6, 9, 10
    Use external 5 V supply if servos jitter — share GND with Arduino.
  3. Connect joystick
    VRx to A0, VRy to A1, SW optional on pin 2. VCC 5 V.
  4. Map joystick to angles
    map(analogRead(A0), 0, 1023, 0, 180) for base. Limit shoulder/elbow ranges to avoid crash.
  5. Program gripper toggle
    Press joystick button: gripper 40° closed / 120° open.
  6. Calibrate home pose
    All servos at safe angles before power each session.
  7. Pick-and-place trial
    Time yourself moving 3 objects. Improve sequence planning on paper first.

Code to upload

Joystick arm control (Arduino C)

#include <Servo.h>
Servo base, shoulder, gripper;

void setup(){
  base.attach(5); shoulder.attach(6); gripper.attach(9);
}

void loop(){
  int x = analogRead(A0);
  int y = analogRead(A1);
  base.write(map(x,0,1023,0,180));
  shoulder.write(map(y,0,1023,30,150));
  delay(15);
}

name: Light-Following Robot
description: Program a robot that drives toward a flashlight beam using two LDR sensors on the front corners.
guide:
What you will build

A small two-motor robot that steers toward light — like plants growing toward the sun — using left and right LDR readings.

What you will learn

  • How differential light sensing steers direction
  • How phototropism in biology relates to robot behaviour
  • How to tune motor speeds for smooth tracking

You did it when…

  • Robot moves toward a torch held 1 m away
  • It corrects when light moves left or right
  • It stops or slows in darkness (optional)

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Mount LDRs on front left and right
    Each with 10 kΩ divider to A0 and A1. Shade sensors with small cardboard tubes to focus light.
  2. Wire motor driver
    Same L298N setup as line-follower project.
  3. Read both sensors
    Print values. Shine torch on left only — left reading should exceed right.
  4. Steering logic
    If left > right + margin: turn left while moving. If right > left: turn right. If similar: go straight.
  5. Darkness behaviour
    If both below threshold, stop motors (no false wandering).
  6. Chase test
    Partner moves torch slowly; robot follows across floor.

Code to upload

Light seeker (Arduino C)

const int LDR_L=A0, LDR_R=A1;
// add motor functions from your chassis project

void loop(){
  int l=analogRead(LDR_L), r=analogRead(LDR_R);
  if(l<80 && r<80){ /* stop */ }
  else if(l>r+30){ /* turn left + forward */ }
  else if(r>l+30){ /* turn right + forward */ }
  else { /* forward */ }
  delay(50);
}

name: Mobile App with MIT App Inventor
description: Create a simple Android app with buttons, text-to-speech, and a counter using MIT App Inventor blocks.
guide:
What you will build

A “STEM Helper” app with a label, two buttons (Speak greeting / Count +1), and a score display you test on a phone or emulator.

What you will learn

  • How mobile UIs combine buttons, labels, and layouts
  • How block-based coding handles events like Button.Click
  • How apps are tested on real devices with AI Companion

You did it when…

  • App installs and opens on phone via MIT AI Companion
  • Speak button reads text aloud
  • Counter button increases number on screen

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Create MIT App Inventor account
    Go to appinventor.mit.edu and sign in with Google.
  2. New project “STEM Helper”
    In Designer, drag a Label, two Buttons, and a HorizontalArrangement if needed.
  3. Rename components
    btnSpeak, btnCount, lblScore, lblGreeting for clarity in Blocks.
  4. Set lblScore text to 0
    In Designer properties panel.
  5. Blocks: btnSpeak.Click
    use TextToSpeech.speak with text “Welcome to STEM Lab”.
  6. Blocks: btnCount.Click
    set lblScore.Text to lblScore.Text + 1 (use math block).
  7. Connect phone
    Install MIT AI2 Companion. Scan QR code from Connect menu. Live test.
  8. Build APK (optional)
    Export .apk to install without Companion if teacher allows.

name: Scratch Animation Story
description: Create an animated story in Scratch with at least two characters, scene changes, dialogue, and sound effects.
guide:
What you will build

A 30–60 second animated story (e.g. “A seed grows into a plant”) with two sprites, backdrop changes, speech bubbles, and background music.

What you will learn

  • How sprites, costumes, and backdrops tell a story
  • How broadcast messages coordinate multiple characters
  • How timing blocks (wait, glide) create smooth animation

You did it when…

  • Story has clear beginning, middle, and end
  • At least two backdrops switch during the story
  • Characters speak or think text on screen

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Plan story on paper
    3 scenes: setup, problem, resolution. Note which sprite acts in each.
  2. Choose sprites and backdrops
    e.g. seed sprite, sun sprite, soil → garden → sunny sky backdrops.
  3. Scene 1 — green flag
    When green flag clicked, switch to backdrop 1, hide seed underground (y position).
  4. Animate growth
    repeat 10: change y by 5, next costume, wait 0.2 seconds.
  5. Broadcast scene changes
    broadcast “scene2” — sun sprite enters; backdrop switches on receive.
  6. Add dialogue
    say block for 2 seconds: “I need water!” — coordinate with wait blocks.
  7. Sound and music
    play sound when rain appears; loop soft music in background sprite.
  8. Share project
    Save to account, copy link, present to class in 1 minute.

name: Fibonacci in Nature Investigation
description: Find and photograph Fibonacci patterns in plants, measure spirals, and calculate ratios close to the golden ratio.
guide:
What you will build

A nature maths portfolio with photos of pinecones, flowers, or shells, spiral counts, and a table of Fibonacci ratios approaching 1.618.

What you will learn

  • How Fibonacci sequence 1,1,2,3,5,8… builds from sums
  • How ratios of consecutive terms approach φ (golden ratio)
  • How mathematics describes patterns in living things

You did it when…

  • You documented at least 3 natural specimens with photos
  • You counted spirals going two directions on a pinecone or sunflower
  • You calculated two ratios of consecutive Fibonacci numbers above 1.6

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Write Fibonacci sequence to 21
    1,1,2,3,5,8,13,21. Calculate 8÷5, 13÷8, 21÷13 — notice values near 1.618.
  2. Collect specimens
    Bring pinecone, sunflower head photo, or shell. Handle plants respectfully — do not destroy school garden.
  3. Count spirals
    On pinecone, count clockwise spirals and anticlockwise spirals. Often consecutive Fibonacci numbers (e.g. 8 and 13).
  4. Photograph and label
    Print or paste photos with captions: location, date, spiral counts.
  5. Measure flower petals
    Many flowers have 3, 5, 8, or 13 petals — record examples.
  6. Write conclusion
    Explain why nature might favour efficient packing (optional: research phyllotaxis in one paragraph).

name: Cryptography and Code Breaking
description: Encrypt and decrypt secret messages using Caesar and substitution ciphers, then crack a partner's code.
guide:
What you will build

A coded message system: you encrypt a short note with a Caesar shift, swap with a partner, and attempt to break each other's cipher without the key.

What you will learn

  • How substitution ciphers map letters to other letters
  • How frequency analysis helps break simple codes
  • How modern encryption protects digital communication

You did it when…

  • You encrypted a 20-letter message with shift 3 (or chosen key)
  • Partner decrypted correctly when given the key
  • You cracked a shift cipher without key using frequency or trial (shift 1–25)

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Make Caesar wheel (optional)
    Two paper circles — inner alphabet, outer shifted. Pin through centre.
  2. Encrypt message
    Choose shift n. A→D if n=3. Write ciphertext in groups of 4 letters.
  3. Exchange with partner
    Pass ciphertext only — keep key secret initially.
  4. Decrypt with key
    Shift letters backward by n. Verify readable English emerges.
  5. Frequency attack
    In English, E is most common. Count letters in ciphertext — guess shift from most frequent letter mapping to E.
  6. Substitution challenge (extension)
    Create random letter mapping table. Harder to break — discuss why computers need strong keys.
  7. Reflect
    One paragraph: why Caesar cipher is weak for real secrets today.

name: Rubber Band Powered Aircraft
description: Build a lightweight balsa or foam aircraft powered by a twisted rubber band and measure flight duration.
guide:
What you will build

A small propeller aircraft storing energy in a wound rubber band that flies in circles or straight lines when released.

What you will learn

  • How elastic potential energy converts to kinetic energy
  • How wing dihedral adds stability
  • How thrust from propeller must balance drag

Safety first

  • Fly outdoors away from faces and roads
  • Do not over-wind rubber band until it snaps — wear eye protection

You did it when…

  • Plane flies at least 5 seconds on one winding
  • You recorded three flight times and averaged them
  • You adjusted wing angle or propeller pitch and retested

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Cut fuselage and wings from balsa
    Lightweight strip body ~30 cm, wing span ~35 cm with slight upward bend (dihedral).
  2. Mount propeller and rubber motor
    Hook rubber band from rear peg to prop shaft. Wind by turning prop counter-clockwise (usually 50–80 turns max).
  3. Add tail surfaces
    Horizontal stabiliser and small vertical fin for straight flight.
  4. Balance weight
    Add clay on nose if plane stalls (nose up). Remove clay if it dives.
  5. Glide test without winding
    Toss gently — should glide flat. Adjust surfaces before powered flight.
  6. Powered flights
    Release at shoulder height. Time with stopwatch. Record in table.
  7. Improve
    Sand prop edges, align thrust line with fuselage. Note one change that increased flight time.

name: Straw Rocket Launcher
description: Design paper rockets launched through a straw by blowing, then optimise fins and nose shape for maximum distance.
guide:
What you will build

A paper rocket that slides over a drinking straw, launched by blowing, with optional fins — you test which design flies farthest.

What you will learn

  • How airflow and pressure create thrust
  • How nose shape and fins affect stability
  • How to run fair comparison tests

Safety first

  • Do not aim at people — blow only toward open end of launch zone
  • One person launches at a time

You did it when…

  • Three rocket designs each flown 5 times with distances recorded
  • Winning design identified with reason (e.g. tighter wrap, smaller fins)
  • Average distance calculated for best rocket

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Make launch straw
    Use sturdy drinking straw taped to desk edge at horizontal angle.
  2. Rocket body
    Roll narrow paper tube loose enough to slide on straw, tape seam. Seal front into point — nose cone.
  3. Design B — add fins
    Cut three small fins from paper, tape at rear evenly spaced.
  4. Design C — your variation
    Try larger fins or blunt nose. Predict which flies farther before testing.
  5. Standard launch
    Slide rocket on straw, blow sharp puff from rear. Measure landing distance from desk.
  6. Record and average
    Table: trial, design, distance. Average per design.
  7. Conclusion
    Explain stability vs drag trade-off in 3–4 sentences.

name: Mini Robot Bug (Vibrating)
description: Build a tiny vibrating bristle bot from a motor, battery, and toothbrush head that skitters across the table.
guide:
What you will build

A small “bug” made from a toothbrush head, coin cell battery, and vibration motor that moves randomly when switched on.

What you will learn

  • How off-centre mass motors create vibration
  • How simple closed circuits power wearables
  • How weight distribution changes movement path

Safety first

  • Adult supervision if soldering coin cell holder
  • Do not short battery with bare wire — it heats quickly
  • Keep hair and loose clothing away from spinning motor

You did it when…

  • Bug vibrates and moves on smooth table for at least 10 seconds
  • Switch or tape contact reliably turns motor on/off
  • You tested two bristle orientations and compared paths

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Cut toothbrush head
    Trim to small oval — bristles point down as “legs”.
  2. Mount vibration motor
    Hot-glue motor on top with eccentric weight clear of surfaces. Angle slightly for curved paths.
  3. Wire battery
    Tape coin cell between motor leads: one lead always touching +, other lead as switch you press to GND side.
  4. Test on table
    Smooth surface works best. If it tips, lower centre of gravity with more glue.
  5. Decorate
    Add googly eyes or pipe cleaner antennae — keep weight light.
  6. Race classmates
    Mark finish line 50 cm away. Three trials — note if straight or spiral path wins.
  7. Explain motion
    Draw force arrows: vibration → friction → sliding in random directions.
